passage:
Mentor's note, Monday after the Diwali break.
Kamal came to our weekly check-in still rattled. At a family dinner, two uncles and his cousin spoke strongly in favour of the new expressway through the wetland near their town. Kamal said he "couldn't believe" anyone reasonable supported it. He told me, "Literally everyone I know thinks it's a disaster." When I asked who "everyone" was, he listed his environment club, his flatmates and the people he follows online. He paused after that. He admitted his uncles drive trucks on that route every week and had reasons he hadn't heard before. He was still upset, and I didn't try to change his view. We agreed he'd phone one uncle and ask him to explain the road from his side, and just listen.
Rukmini

qa.q: Who did Kamal list when asked who "everyone" was?
qa.a: His environment club, his flatmates and the people he follows online.

qa.q: Why was Kamal so shocked at the family dinner?
qa.a: Almost everyone he talks to opposes the expressway, so he'd come to feel his view was what all reasonable people think, and his uncles broke that picture.

qa.q: Why is phoning one uncle and just listening a good next step?
qa.a: It lets Kamal hear reasons from someone outside his usual circle without turning it into another argument.

qa.q: How might Kamal's uncles have experienced that dinner?
qa.a: They might have felt judged by a younger relative who assumed their view was unreasonable, when for them the road is part of their weekly work.

grounding: It shows a young man whose like-minded circle made his view feel universal, shocked by different views at a family dinner.

passage:
Sunday, late
Still annoyed. At Tarun's engagement lunch someone brought up the firecracker ban for Diwali, and I said, "Obviously it should be banned, everyone agrees on that now." The table went silent. Then Tarun's father said it's their family tradition, and they buy from a small shop in Sivakasi that feeds a whole street. Tarun's grandmother said the children wait all year for it. Even Tarun said a total ban felt unfair to him. Ajji leaned over and whispered, "My boy, not at an engagement."
I honestly thought this was settled. In my college group nobody even argues about it; we share the air-quality posts and move on. I felt ambushed, and a bit stupid for saying "everyone".
Maybe my "everyone" is just forty people who think exactly like me. That's an uncomfortable thought.
- Nilesh

qa.q: What did Tarun's father say about the firecrackers?
qa.a: That it's their family tradition, and they buy from a small shop in Sivakasi that feeds a whole street.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh feel ambushed at the lunch?
qa.a: He truly believed the question was settled because nobody in his college group argues about it, so disagreement from family felt like a surprise attack.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do with his uncomfortable thought?
qa.a: He could ask Tarun and his father about their reasons over tea, and talk to people outside his college group before saying 'everyone'.

qa.q: How might Tarun's grandmother have felt when Nilesh called the ban obvious?
qa.a: She might feel that something the children look forward to all year was being dismissed without a thought.

grounding: It shows a young man who mostly meets like-minded friends assuming his view is universal and being shocked at a family gathering.

The wedding lunch in Tikamgarh was spread on long mats under a shamiana, and Devesh, twenty-one, home from college in Delhi, was on his third puri when someone mentioned the new dam upriver.
"That dam is a disaster," he said. "Everyone knows it. Villages drowned, forests gone. Nobody our age supports it."
His cousin Vandana put down her glass. "I'm our age. I support it."
Madhuri Chachi nodded. "Our fields dry out every May, beta. The canal will reach us."
Two uncles agreed with her. Even the cook, refilling the dal, said the dam meant water.
Devesh looked around the mat. At college, every single person he talked to had signed the petition against it. "You're all serious?"
"Very serious," Vandana said. "You've been in Delhi too long."
He ate the rest of his puri in silence, stunned.

qa.q: What did Madhuri Chachi say happens to their fields every May?
qa.a: She said their fields dry out every May.

qa.q: Why was Devesh so shocked by his family's views?
qa.a: Everyone he talked to at college had signed the petition, so he felt his opinion was nearly universal and didn't expect people at home, facing dry fields, to see it differently.

qa.q: What could Devesh do next instead of eating in silence?
qa.a: He could ask Vandana and Chachi why the canal matters to them, and treat his surprise as a sign that he has only been hearing one side.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Devesh's claim that nobody their age supports the dam?
qa.a: Vandana finds it out of touch, as her line about Delhi shows, because she and many at home live with the dry fields every year.

passage:
At Sunday lunch in his grandmother's Toronto apartment, Yosef, twenty, finally had a chance to talk about the city's plan to close downtown to cars on weekends.
"It's so obvious," he said, cutting his chicken. "Quieter streets, cleaner air. Literally everyone supports it."
His grandmother set down her fork. "I don't. How would I get to the synagogue with my knees?"
"Grandma, you'd take the bus."
"Two buses," said Uncle Avi. "And my shop is downtown. Weekend customers come by car."
Ada, his sister, gave him a look. "Yosef, everyone in your university housing supports it. That's not literally everyone."
Yosef felt his face go hot. In his group chats, in his classes, at every café he went to, nobody had said a word against the plan. He sat back in his chair, genuinely stunned.

qa.q: Why did Yosef's grandmother say she doesn't support the plan?
qa.a: She asked how she would get to the synagogue with her knees.

qa.q: Why did Yosef believe "literally everyone" supported the plan?
qa.a: In his group chats, classes and cafés nobody had spoken against it, so living among like-minded people made his view feel almost universal.

qa.q: What could Yosef do with the surprise he felt at lunch?
qa.a: He could treat it as a clue that his circle is narrow, and ask his grandmother and Uncle Avi more about their needs before arguing again.

qa.q: How does Ada see Yosef's claim?
qa.a: Ada sees that Yosef mistook his university crowd for everyone, and seems to want him to notice it before the lunch becomes an argument.

Note to myself after Sunday lunch. Sharmila.
Santosh came home from his Bengaluru college for the holiday, and at lunch the talk turned to the plan to build a bus depot on the old lake bed. Santosh laughed and said, "Obviously no one supports that. It's destroying a lake." His Chacha said he supported it: the depot would bring jobs and cut his commute. My husband agreed. Santosh looked at them as if they had grown horns. "Seriously? Everyone I know is against it." He meant his hostel and his environment club, I think. He went quiet, then argued too sharply, and left the table before the kheer. I found him on the terrace later and asked how many people he knew who ride the bus to work. None, he said. I told him that's worth thinking about, and that his view is still worth arguing for, calmly.

qa.q: What was planned for the old lake bed?
qa.a: A bus depot was planned for the old lake bed.

qa.q: Why was Santosh so shocked when Chacha supported the depot?
qa.a: Santosh felt stunned and a little offended, because everyone he talks to at the hostel and the environment club is against it, so his view seemed universal.

qa.q: What did Sharmila's question on the terrace help Santosh see, and what could he do next?
qa.a: It showed that he knows nobody who rides the bus to work; next he could ask Chacha why he supports the depot and argue his own view calmly.

qa.q: How might Chacha have seen Santosh's reaction at lunch?
qa.a: Chacha may have felt dismissed, since jobs and a shorter commute were real reasons that Santosh treated as unthinkable.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose circle all agree assuming his view is universal and being shocked by relatives' different views at a family lunch.

passage:
Cousin Rupal's wedding, day 2, very late.
Had the weirdest conversation at the sangeet. I said to Keerthana, half joking, "Thank god our generation is done with arranged marriages, right?" I thought that was just a fact. Everyone in my college group says it. Keerthana looked at me for a long second and said her parents are finding someone for her and she's actually glad about it. That she trusts them, and likes that it's not all on her. Then Mausi joined in, and two cousins, and suddenly I was the odd one out at my own family's wedding. My ears went hot. I argued too much. I think I actually said "that's backwards", which, ugh.
Here's the thing I keep turning over: I don't know a single person who thinks like Keerthana. Or I didn't, until tonight.
Nitin

qa.q: At which event did Nitin talk with Keerthana?
qa.a: At the sangeet, on day 2 of cousin Rupal's wedding.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's answer leave Nitin so shaken?
qa.a: Nitin felt shocked and embarrassed, because everyone in Nitin's college group agrees, so that view had seemed like a simple fact.

qa.q: What could Nitin do the next time a family conversation turns to opinions like this?
qa.a: Ask people what they think and why before stating something as obvious, and listen without calling it backwards.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when Nitin said 'that's backwards'?
qa.a: Keerthana may have felt judged and hurt, since she trusts her parents and is glad about her choice.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose friends all agree assuming the view is universal and being shocked by relatives' different views at a family wedding.

passage: Karthik had spent two years at an engineering college in Chennai, where everyone he knew thought the new expressway through their home district was a brilliant idea. Faster travel, jobs, progress. His hostel friends agreed, his online groups agreed. So at the Pongal gathering in his family's village near Tiruvannamalai, he said so, loudly, over lunch. The room went quiet. His aunt Sarita put down her plate. "The expressway will take our mango grove." An uncle said it would cut the village in two. His grandfather said the old road had done fine for sixty years. Karthik felt stunned. He had thought almost everyone agreed. He had honestly never met anyone who didn't. He sat through the rest of lunch hot-faced and quiet. Later, Sarita aunty walked him to the grove. "Just listen, before you decide we're all wrong," she said.

qa.q: What did Sarita aunty say the expressway would take?
qa.a: Our mango grove.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as the room went quiet?
qa.a: He felt stunned and embarrassed, since he had believed almost everyone agreed with him.

qa.q: What could Karthik do before the next family gathering?
qa.a: Ask relatives what they think and listen, as Sarita aunty suggested, instead of assuming his college friends' view is everyone's.

qa.q: How does Sarita aunty see the expressway?
qa.a: She sees it as a threat to the family's mango grove, not as progress.

grounding: Shows a young adult who mostly meets like-minded people assuming his view is nearly universal and being shocked at a family gathering.

passage: Tuan had lived in Melbourne for three years, studying and sharing a flat with students who all believed a four-day work week was obviously the future. Everyone he followed online said so. At his cousin's wedding in Sydney, he mentioned it at dinner as if it were settled. "Everyone thinks five days is outdated, right?" Siddiq, his cousin's husband, laughed, then saw Tuan was serious. "I run a bakery. Four days would kill it." An aunt said her hospital couldn't close a day. An uncle said he'd love it, but his factory never would. Tuan felt his face burn. He had been so sure. On the train home, he realised that in three years he had barely talked to anyone outside his university. Everyone he knew thought like him because he'd chosen them that way. He opened his phone and followed Siddiq's bakery page.

qa.q: What does Siddiq run?
qa.a: A bakery.

qa.q: What was Tuan feeling when relatives disagreed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face burning, because he had been sure almost everyone agreed with him.

qa.q: What did Tuan realise on the train, and what small step did he take?
qa.a: That he had barely talked to anyone outside university; he followed Siddiq's bakery page to hear other views.

qa.q: How might Siddiq see Tuan's comment?
qa.a: Siddiq first found it funny, then saw that a four-day week would hurt his bakery, so to him it's far from obvious.

passage:
Saurabh,
Back from my cousin's wedding in Kottayam and still a bit shaken. You know how at uni everyone, literally everyone, thinks the city should ban private cars from the old town? Our whole group, the debate society, the people I follow online. I honestly thought it was just common sense by now.
So at lunch I said it, casually, like saying the sky is blue. My uncle put his spoon down. He runs a small shop in the old market, and his customers come by car. An aunt said the buses there are useless at night for women. My grandfather said I was living in a bubble.
I was shocked. Then annoyed. Then, lying awake, a bit embarrassed. My "everyone" is about forty people who study the same subject in the same city.
I still think I'm partly right. But I'd never have heard any of this in Delhi.
Thomas

qa.a: Thomas felt shocked and then embarrassed, having assumed the car-ban view was common sense because everyone at uni shared it.

qa.a: Thomas could ask the uncle and aunt more about the shop and the night buses, and seek out people outside the uni group before assuming a view is universal.

qa.a: The uncle may feel worried and a bit dismissed, since his small shop depends on customers who come by car.

passage:
Kalyani, you asked what happened at Diwali dinner. Okay. I'm Sachin, and I made a fool of myself.
Everyone at my college thinks arranged marriage is outdated. My flatmates, my class, every reel I scroll past. So when Mausi asked about my plans, I said, "Nobody my age wants an arranged marriage any more. That's over."
And my cousin, who's twenty-three and an engineer, said, "I want one. My parents know me. I trust them to help." Her brother agreed. Then my own sister said she hadn't decided.
I felt my face go hot. I'd said "nobody" like it was a fact. Turns out I'd just never asked anyone outside my flat.
I still know what I want for myself. But I've stopped saying "nobody" and "everybody". At the next dinner I'm going to ask more and announce less.

qa.q: How old is the cousin who wants an arranged marriage?
qa.a: The cousin is twenty-three and an engineer.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when the cousin disagreed?
qa.a: Sachin felt embarrassed and caught out, having said 'nobody' as if it were a fact.

qa.q: What does Sachin plan for the next dinner, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To ask more and announce less, because Sachin's college circle turned out not to speak for the family.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt hearing Sachin's claim?
qa.a: The cousin may have felt dismissed, since the word 'nobody' erased her own wish, so she spoke up.

grounding: Shows a young adult who, surrounded by like-minded friends, assumed a view was universal and was surprised at a family dinner.

Sunday. At his Bua's house in Ludhiana for the Gurpurab lunch, he repeated the rant to the family. His Phuphad ji said, "That flyover saves me an hour a day to the factory." His cousin, a truck driver, said the old road had nearly killed him twice. Gurpreet sat back, stunned. It felt as if they were ganging up on him.
Wednesday. He told Irfan in the canteen. Irfan shrugged. "Your forty likes are forty hostel kids who walk everywhere. Your family drives every day."
Gurpreet was quiet for a moment. "So I don't actually know what most people think."
"Nobody does," Irfan said. "That's why you ask."

passage: Gurleen, you came back from that wedding saying, "How can anyone in our family think that?" Sit, have some plum cake, it's Christmas. At twenty, I was the same. In college in Bangalore, all my friends read the same papers and argued only with people who already agreed. I was sure every sensible person thought as I did about the city elections. Then at Christmas lunch in Kottayam, my own uncle said the opposite, calmly, over the appam. I was so shocked I dropped my spoon. I called him old-fashioned, in front of everyone. Later my grandmother told me he had lost his shop when the new rules came in. He had reasons I had never heard, because I had never listened to anyone like him. So, Gurleen, before you call someone foolish, ask them why. That is Joseph uncle's Christmas lesson, learned the hard way.
